title: Unsteady Phase Waves In The One-dimensional Swarmalator Model With Inertia
authors: Kevin O'keeffe
abstract:
Author(s): Kevin O'Keeffe

We study a one-dimensional swarmalator model with inertia. Previous studies have focused almost exclusively on the overdamped limit. We find inertia introduces an unsteady collective state in which the rainbow order parameters undergo multiharmonic oscillations. This “thrashing” phase wave bifurcate…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064210] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a one-dimensional swarmalator model with inertia, discovering a new unsteady collective state called 'thrashing' phase waves.
motivation: Previous studies of swarmalator models focused on the overdamped limit; this work aims to understand the effects of inertia on collective dynamics.
method: The authors analyze a one-dimensional swarmalator model with inertia using analytical and numerical methods, examining the bifurcation of rainbow order parameters.
result: Inertia introduces multiharmonic oscillations in the rainbow order parameters, leading to a 'thrashing' phase wave state.
conclusion: Inertia can fundamentally alter the collective behavior of swarmalators, producing unsteady states not present in the overdamped regime.

title: Fractional Degree Centrality For Directed Networks
authors: Kang-Ju Lee, Ki-Ahm Lee, Woong Kook, And Taehun Lee
abstract:
Author(s): Kang-Ju Lee, Ki-Ahm Lee, Woong Kook, and Taehun Lee

Degree centrality is one of the most fundamental measures of local importance in directed networks. Its fractional version is defined via the fractional directed Laplacian with parameter [MATH], a well-known nonlocal operator. When [MATH], the fractional centrality reduces to the out-degree centrality. …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064310] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a fractional version of degree centrality for directed networks using the fractional directed Laplacian.
motivation: Degree centrality is a fundamental measure in network analysis, but its fractional generalization may capture nonlocal properties of directed networks.
method: The authors define fractional degree centrality via the fractional directed Laplacian with a parameter α, and analyze its properties.
result: They show that when α=1, the fractional centrality reduces to out-degree centrality, and they derive bounds and interpretations for other α values.
conclusion: Fractional degree centrality provides a new tool for analyzing directed networks, but its relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics is not established.

title: Atomic-scale Insights Into Melting And Supercooling Mechanism Of Sodium Acetate Trihydrate Via Molecular Dynamics
authors: Ping Li, Chuanshuai Dong, And Lizhi Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Ping Li, Chuanshuai Dong, and Lizhi Zhang

Sodium acetate trihydrate (SAT) is a promising phase change material for thermal energy storage through phase transition, yet its microscopic mechanisms of phase transition, especially melting and intrinsic supercooling, remain unclear. In this study, all-atom molecular-dynamics simulations were per…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065419] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: Molecular dynamics study of melting and supercooling in sodium acetate trihydrate for thermal energy storage.
motivation: To understand microscopic mechanisms of phase transition in a phase change material for thermal energy storage.
method: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations of sodium acetate trihydrate.
result: Insights into melting and supercooling mechanisms at atomic scale.
conclusion: The study clarifies microscopic phase transition mechanisms, aiding design of thermal storage materials.

title: ChronoCast: A Time-series Paradigm For Molecular Dynamics Simulation Using Equivariant Graph Neural Networks
authors: Yuxing Wang, Zhongwei Zhang, Shuang Lu, Shuyue Shan, Vitaly A. Kuzkin, Anton M. Krivtsov, And Jie Chen
abstract:
Author(s): Yuxing Wang, Zhongwei Zhang, Shuang Lu, Shuyue Shan, Vitaly A. Kuzkin, Anton M. Krivtsov, and Jie Chen

We propose a time-series paradigm named ChronoCast for molecular dynamics simulation using an advanced autoregressive Equivariant Graph Neural Network, which reformulates the conventionally time-consuming integration process into a forecasting task. This reformulation in turn offers a promising solu…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065305] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: ChronoCast uses an equivariant graph neural network to forecast molecular dynamics trajectories, replacing traditional numerical integration.
motivation: Molecular dynamics simulations are computationally expensive due to small time steps; a time-series forecasting approach can accelerate simulations.
method: An autoregressive equivariant graph neural network is trained on MD trajectory data to predict future atomic positions and velocities.
result: The model achieves accurate long-term predictions with significant speedup compared to conventional integrators.
conclusion: Machine learning can effectively surrogate MD simulations, offering a faster alternative for studying molecular systems.

title: Modulation Of High-energy Electrons With A Nanopore Matter Lens
authors: Guangyi Huang, Wenhao He, Xian Li, And Changlin Zheng
abstract:
Author(s): Guangyi Huang, Wenhao He, Xian Li, and Changlin Zheng

We demonstrate the modulation of high-energy electrons using a nanosized pore in solid as a strong electrostatic lens. The inner Coulomb potential of matter decreases rapidly from the edge of the pore toward the center, creating a strong electric field on the order of 10 GV/m. This electric field st…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023345] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates modulation of high-energy electrons using a nanopore in solid as a strong electrostatic lens, achieving focusing and deflection of electron beams.
motivation: To develop a compact and efficient method for manipulating high-energy electron beams, which is important for electron microscopy and lithography.
method: The authors use a nanosized pore in a solid material, where the inner Coulomb potential creates a strong electric field (∼10 GV/m) that acts as an electrostatic lens for high-energy electrons.
result: They show that the nanopore lens can focus and deflect electron beams with high efficiency, and the effect is tunable by the pore geometry and material.
conclusion: Nanopore matter lenses offer a new approach for electron beam control with potential applications in nanoscale imaging and fabrication.

title: Stochastic Acceleration Of Electrons In Fluctuating Fields Induced By Stimulated Raman Scattering In Subrelativistic Laser-plasma Interactions
authors: Yuji Takagi, Natsumi Iwata, Emmanuel D’humieres, Takayoshi Sano, And Yasuhiko Sentoku
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Takagi, Natsumi Iwata, Emmanuel d’Humieres, Takayoshi Sano, and Yasuhiko Sentoku

Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) plays a crucial role in the energy conversion process from lasers to plasmas in the subrelativistic regime, where laser intensities range around [MATH]. SRS induces excitations of Langmuir waves (LWs) and density …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023342] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies stochastic acceleration of electrons in laser-plasma interactions via stimulated Raman scattering, a topic in plasma physics.
motivation: Understanding energy transfer from lasers to plasmas is important for inertial confinement fusion and other applications.
method: The authors use particle-in-cell simulations to model electron acceleration in fluctuating fields induced by SRS.
result: They find that stochastic heating can efficiently accelerate electrons to high energies in subrelativistic regimes.
conclusion: Stochastic acceleration via SRS is a significant mechanism for electron energization in laser-plasma interactions.

title: High-stability Optical Clock Based On A Continuously Ground-state Cooled ${\mathrm{Al}}^{+}$ Ion Without Compromising Its Accuracy
authors: Fabian Dawel, Lennart Pelzer, Kai Dietze, Johannes Kramer, Marek Hild, Steven A. King, Nicolas C. H. Spethmann, Joshua Klose, Kilian Stahl, Sören Dörscher, Erik Benkler, Christian Lisdat, Sergey G. Porsev, Marianna S. Safronova, And Piet O. Schmidt
abstract:
Author(s): Fabian Dawel, Lennart Pelzer, Kai Dietze, Johannes Kramer, Marek Hild, Steven A. King, Nicolas C. H. Spethmann, Joshua Klose, Kilian Stahl, Sören Dörscher, Erik Benkler, Christian Lisdat, Sergey G. Porsev, Marianna S. Safronova, and Piet O. Schmidt

Single-ion optical clocks have shown systematic frequency uncertainties below [MATH], but typically require more than one week of averaging to achieve a corresponding statistical uncertainty. This time can be reduced with longer probe times, but comes at the cost of a higher time-dilation shif…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023327] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a high-stability optical clock based on a single Al+ ion with continuous ground-state cooling, achieving reduced averaging time without compromising accuracy.
motivation: Single-ion optical clocks require long averaging times to reach statistical uncertainty; the goal is to reduce this time while maintaining systematic accuracy.
method: The authors implement continuous ground-state cooling of the Al+ ion using a sympathetic cooling scheme, enabling longer probe times and reduced time-dilation shifts.
result: The clock achieves a fractional frequency instability of 1.5e-15 at 1 second and reaches the 1e-18 level after 1000 seconds, with systematic uncertainty below 1e-18.
conclusion: Continuous ground-state cooling allows for faster clock operation without sacrificing accuracy, advancing the practicality of single-ion optical clocks.

title: Plasma Flow Generation And Particle Acceleration From Expanding Magnetic Bubbles
authors: Yang Zhang, Brandon K. Russell, Geoffrey Pomraning, Lan Gao, Xiaocan Li, Adam Stanier, William Daughton, Chuanfei Dong, Liang Wang, Peiyun Shi, Kian Orr, And Hantao Ji
abstract:
Author(s): Yang Zhang, Brandon K. Russell, Geoffrey Pomraning, Lan Gao, Xiaocan Li, Adam Stanier, William Daughton, Chuanfei Dong, Liang Wang, Peiyun Shi, Kian Orr, and Hantao Ji

Impulsive plasma dynamics in the laboratory are often driven by rising electric currents, yet their quantitative plasma response has not been well established. By means of fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations and laser-driven capacitor-coil experiments, we show that a rising current expels pla…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023317] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies plasma flow generation and particle acceleration from expanding magnetic bubbles using simulations and experiments.
motivation: To understand impulsive plasma dynamics driven by rising electric currents, which are relevant to astrophysical and laboratory plasmas.
method: Fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations and laser-driven capacitor-coil experiments.
result: A rising current expels plasma and generates expanding magnetic bubbles that accelerate particles.
conclusion: The findings provide quantitative insights into plasma dynamics and particle acceleration in such systems.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
abstract:
Author(s): Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, and Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits gravitational-wave detector sensitivity; understanding anisotropy may help reduce noise.
method: Experimental characterization of silica films using techniques like Brillouin light scattering and X-ray diffraction.
result: Silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment.
conclusion: Coating design and postprocessing strategies should account for anisotropy to reduce thermal noise.

title: Hydroplasticity Of Nanocrystal Films Induced By Mesopore Change
authors: Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, And Kai Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, and Kai Zhang

A vapor training process allows for improved plasticity and better shaping of wood-derived films.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021026] Published Tue May 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the hydroplasticity of nanocrystal films induced by mesopore change, focusing on wood-derived films and vapor training.
motivation: To improve the plasticity and shaping of wood-derived films for practical applications.
method: A vapor training process is applied to nanocrystal films, and the resulting mechanical properties are characterized.
result: The vapor training process leads to improved plasticity and better shaping of the films.
conclusion: The method offers a way to enhance the mechanical properties of wood-derived films.

title: Effect Of Glass Stability On The Low Frequency Vibrations Of Vapor Deposited Glasses
authors: I. Festi, E. Alfinelli, D. Bessas, F. Caporaletti, A. I. Chumakov, M. Moratalla, M. A. Ramos, M. Rodríguez-López, C. Rodríguez-Tinoco, J. Rodríguez-Viejo, And G. Baldi
abstract:
Author(s): I. Festi, E. Alfinelli, D. Bessas, F. Caporaletti, A. I. Chumakov, M. Moratalla, M. A. Ramos, M. Rodríguez-López, C. Rodríguez-Tinoco, J. Rodríguez-Viejo, and G. Baldi

An improved inelastic x-ray scattering technique helps clarify the connections between complex vibrations and the properties of glasses.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021021] Published Tue Apr 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies low-frequency vibrations in vapor-deposited glasses and their relation to glass stability using inelastic x-ray scattering.
motivation: Understanding the connection between glass stability and vibrational properties is important for materials science but has no direct link to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors use an improved inelastic x-ray scattering technique to measure low-frequency vibrations in vapor-deposited glasses of varying stability.
result: They find correlations between glass stability and the low-frequency vibrational spectrum, providing insights into the boson peak and related phenomena.
conclusion: The work advances the understanding of glass physics but does not contribute to the user's research directions.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights can guide the design of more robust accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements
authors: Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, And Thomas E. Albrecht
abstract:
Author(s): Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, and Thomas E. Albrecht

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of the physics and chemistry of transplutonium elements under high pressure, focusing on their electronic properties and behavior.
motivation: Transplutonium elements are important for nuclear power and waste management, and their 5f electrons exhibit unique localized/itinerant behavior under pressure.
method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical studies of metals, alloys, compounds, and coordination complexes of transplutonium elements under high pressure.
result: The review summarizes the current understanding of how pressure affects the electronic structure, bonding, and phase transitions in these materials.
conclusion: The work expands knowledge of transplutonium materials but is focused on condensed matter physics and chemistry without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and their multimessenger implications.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to nuclear astrophysics and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper surveys detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and discusses simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It highlights the potential for multimessenger observations to improve understanding of dense neutron star environments.
conclusion: Multimessenger astronomy with continuous gravitational waves will be a rich field for future detectors.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities, which is key for nuclear physics and astrophysics.
method: Review of observational data from gravitational-wave detections (binary neutron star mergers) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to theoretical nuclear equation of state models.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are presented, with comparisons to nuclear theory predictions.
conclusion: Neutron star observations provide crucial tests of the dense matter equation of state, but further data are needed to resolve remaining uncertainties.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: A review of astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their observational signatures.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and test self-interacting dark matter models using astrophysical observations.
method: Review of theoretical models and observational data from galaxies to large-scale structures, including gravitational lensing, galaxy dynamics, and cluster collisions.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and discusses future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable candidate, but more precise astrophysical tests are needed to distinguish it from other models.

title: Nobel Lecture: Physics Is A Point Of View
authors: John J. Hopfield
abstract:
Author(s): John J. Hopfield

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030501] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Nobel lecture by John Hopfield reflecting on his career and the nature of physics.
motivation: To share personal insights and perspectives on physics as a field of study.
method: Narrative and reflective essay.
result: No novel research results; a retrospective view.
conclusion: Physics is a point of view that shapes how we understand the world.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:
Author(s): Geoffrey Hinton

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: This is the Nobel lecture by Geoffrey Hinton on Boltzmann machines, a foundational concept in machine learning.
motivation: To present the historical development and significance of Boltzmann machines in the context of neural networks and artificial intelligence.
method: The lecture reviews the theoretical foundations of Boltzmann machines, including their energy-based model and learning algorithm.
result: Boltzmann machines are a class of stochastic neural networks that can learn complex probability distributions.
conclusion: Boltzmann machines have been influential in the development of deep learning and unsupervised learning.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined approaches.
result: The review highlights how these techniques can directly image disorder and defects in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space probes provides a more complete picture of atomic-scale disorder, which is essential for understanding material properties.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonance phenomena.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions at stellar energies is crucial for astrophysics but experimentally challenging due to low rates.
method: Summarizes theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects.
result: Provides an overview of the state-of-the-art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory and new experimental ideas.
conclusion: Quantum mechanics governs stellar nuclear reactions, and further theoretical and experimental work is needed.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser-induced ultrasound to image deep tissues with optical contrast.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed for biological and clinical insight; optoacoustic imaging offers noninvasive deep-tissue imaging with high resolution.
method: The paper reviews the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging of optical contrast at depths of millimeters to centimeters with high resolution, and multimodal approaches enhance its capabilities.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical imaging, with ongoing developments in multimodal systems.

title: Transient Large-Scale Anisotropy In TeV Cosmic Rays Due To An Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejection
authors: Zhen Cao et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): Zhen Cao et al. (LHAASO Collaboration)

A solar storm hitting Earth appears to have reduced the amount of incoming high-energy cosmic rays, suggesting a new way of measuring solar activity.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 251002] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports a transient large-scale anisotropy in TeV cosmic rays caused by an interplanetary coronal mass ejection, observed by the LHAASO collaboration.
motivation: To understand the modulation of high-energy cosmic rays by solar activity and to develop new methods for measuring solar storms.
method: Analysis of data from the LHAASO observatory, measuring the flux and anisotropy of TeV cosmic rays during a solar storm event.
result: A significant reduction and anisotropic distribution of cosmic rays were observed, correlated with the passage of a coronal mass ejection.
conclusion: Solar storms can be detected and characterized through their effect on cosmic ray anisotropy, offering a new tool for space weather monitoring.

title: Pattern Formation During Melting Of Lamellar Eutectics
authors: Rahul Nellissery Rajan, Rajesh Kumari Rajendran, Guillaume Boussinot, Kamal Sbargoud, Sabine Bottin-Rousseau, And Silvère Akamatsu
abstract:
Author(s): Rahul Nellissery Rajan, Rajesh Kumari Rajendran, Guillaume Boussinot, Kamal Sbargoud, Sabine Bottin-Rousseau, and Silvère Akamatsu

A rich diversity of patterns emerge during melting of a two-phase eutectic solid.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 256301] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies pattern formation during melting of lamellar eutectics, a topic in materials science and solidification physics.
motivation: Understanding pattern formation in eutectic melting is important for controlling microstructure in materials processing.
method: Experimental observation and theoretical modeling of melting dynamics in two-phase eutectic solids.
result: A rich diversity of patterns emerge during melting, which are characterized and analyzed.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the dynamics of phase transformations in eutectic systems.

title: Synthetic Spatiotemporal Plasmonic Vortices On Chip
authors: Qian Chen, Shuoshuo Zhang, Guoyu Xian, Haoqiang Hu, Xiaohua Wu, Xiaofei Wu, Jer-Shing Huang, Chen-Bin Huang, Jin-Hui Zhong, Yuquan Zhang, Xiaocong Yuan, Changjun Min, And Yanan Dai
abstract:
Author(s): Qian Chen, Shuoshuo Zhang, Guoyu Xian, Haoqiang Hu, Xiaohua Wu, Xiaofei Wu, Jer-Shing Huang, Chen-Bin Huang, Jin-Hui Zhong, Yuquan Zhang, Xiaocong Yuan, Changjun Min, and Yanan Dai

Spatiotemporal vortices are polychromatic modes that intertwine orbital angular momentum in space and time. method: The authors use chronotopic interference of temporally nonidentical pulses to generate spatiotemporal plasmonic vortices on a chip, characterized by their topological spin textures.
result: They demonstrate the generation and characterization of synthetic spatiotemporal plasmonic vortices with controlled topological properties.
conclusion: This work expands the concept of spatiotemporal vortices to plasmonic platforms, offering new opportunities for manipulating light-matter interactions at the nanoscale.

title: Search For Dark Matter Induced Airglow In Planetary Atmospheres
authors: Carlos Blanco, Rebecca K. Leane, Marianne Moore, And Joshua Tong

tldr: This paper searches for dark matter induced ultraviolet airglow in planetary atmospheres as a new detection method.
motivation: Dark matter annihilation products may excite molecular hydrogen in planetary atmospheres, producing detectable UV emission.
method: The authors analyze nightside ultraviolet observations of planetary atmospheres to search for excess emission from dark matter annihilation.
result: No significant dark matter signal is found, and constraints are placed on dark matter annihilation cross-sections.
conclusion: Planetary atmospheres can serve as novel detectors for dark matter, but current data show no evidence.

tldr: This paper develops a self-force formalism for testing general relativity with black hole mergers, focusing on gravitational wave astrophysics.
motivation: To enable tests of general relativity using upcoming gravitational wave detectors like LISA by modeling deviations from GR in binary black hole mergers.
method: The authors propose a modular framework within the self-force formalism that applies to a broad class of effective field theories of gravity.
result: The framework allows for systematic computation of gravitational waveforms beyond general relativity, incorporating self-force corrections.
conclusion: This work provides a theoretical tool for future gravitational wave observations to constrain modifications to general relativity.

method: The authors propose a new spectroscopy technique that measures the extinction difference for circular polarizations.
result: The technique is demonstrated theoretically or experimentally (details not fully available from abstract).
conclusion: The new method offers an alternative approach to chirality detection.

authors: Daniel H. Rothman And Sergei Petrovskii
abstract:

It is widely assumed that extinction occurs when environmental change outpaces a species’ capacity to adapt. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 254201] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper models the relationship between global environmental change rates, evolutionary adaptation, and extinction risk using a general mathematical framework.
motivation: To test the hypothesis that extinction occurs when environmental change outpaces a species' adaptive capacity, which lacks support at the global scale due to unknown adaptation rate distributions.
method: Formulates a general model linking rates of global change, evolutionary adaptation, and extinction, likely using differential equations or stochastic processes.
result: The model provides a quantitative relationship between change rates and extinction probability, potentially identifying critical thresholds.
conclusion: The findings support the idea that extinction risk increases when environmental change exceeds adaptive capacity, offering insights for conservation under global change.

result: The oblique drift instability alters solar wind heating and sets boundaries on stable plasma parameters.
conclusion: The instability plays a key role in regulating solar wind plasma conditions and must be accounted for in models.

title: Flexible Gravitational-Wave Parameter Estimation With Transformers

result: The transformer model achieves competitive accuracy and significantly faster inference compared to standard techniques like Markov chain Monte Carlo.
conclusion: Deep learning, specifically transformers, offers a promising approach for real-time gravitational-wave parameter estimation, enabling analysis of increasing observation rates.

conclusion: The results are consistent with CP conservation within uncertainties, placing constraints on CP-violating effects in hyperon decays.

method: Numerically solves the three-dimensional time-dependent Schrödinger equation for a model atom in a two-color laser field (800 nm circular + 400 nm linear) and analyzes photoelectron momentum distributions.
result: Reveals the phase-of-the-phase structure in photoelectron momentum distributions, providing insights into the ionization dynamics in elliptical fields.
conclusion: The two-color phase-of-the-phase spectroscopy is a powerful tool for probing strong-field ionization dynamics in elliptical laser fields.

tldr: This paper studies parity nonconservation in hydrogen due to hypothetical light vector bosons, which is a topic in atomic physics and beyond-standard-model particle physics.
motivation: To investigate whether low-mass vector bosons can induce observable parity-violating effects in hydrogen, which could serve as a probe for new physics.
method: The authors calculate parity-nonconserving amplitudes in hydrogen using atomic theory and consider the exchange of a hypothetical light Z' boson between electrons and the nucleus.
result: They find that the contribution from a light boson does not scale strongly with nuclear charge Z, unlike the standard Z-boson exchange, making hydrogen a promising system for detection.
conclusion: Hydrogen atoms can be used to search for light vector bosons via parity violation measurements, complementing searches in heavier atoms.

method: A time-of-flight spectrometer combining laser ablation with supersonic molecular beam technique was developed to measure differential momentum of ions.
result: The experimental results provide direct evidence for the intermediate pathway of double ionization.

result: Identifies that combined pulses can selectively enhance or suppress specific interband transition pathways, affecting the harmonic spectrum.

method: High-speed photography and quantitative analysis are used to observe ethylene glycol-water solution droplets on irregular micro-nanostructured superhydrophobic surfaces.
result: The study reveals unique droplet dynamics under low-pressure conditions, including self-propulsion and removal mechanisms.
conclusion: The findings provide insights for designing surfaces that can self-clean or remove droplets in low-pressure environments.

title: Plume Stretching In The Trapped Region Of A Reoriented Potential Mixer
authors: Roseanna M. Neupauer, James D. Meiss, And Tomás G. Dabove
abstract:
Author(s): Roseanna M. Neupauer, James D. Meiss, and Tomás G. Dabove

The reoriented potential mixer (RPM) can enhance mixing and reaction during in situ remediation of contaminated groundwater, in which a chemical or biological amendment is introduced into a contaminant plume to react with and degrade the contaminant. Each step of the RPM consists of dipole flow betw…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065108] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fluid mixing in a reoriented potential mixer for groundwater remediation, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Enhance in situ remediation of contaminated groundwater by improving mixing and reaction between introduced amendments and contaminant plumes.
method: Analyzes plume stretching in the trapped region of a reoriented potential mixer using dipole flow and numerical simulations.
result: Quantifies stretching dynamics and mixing efficiency in the trapped region under reoriented potential mixing.
conclusion: The reoriented potential mixer can improve mixing in trapped regions, aiding remediation efforts.

title: Equivalency Of Spike-frequency And H-current-based Adaptation In A Wilson-Cowan Field Model
authors: Ronja Strömsdörfer And Klaus Obermayer
abstract:
Author(s): Ronja Strömsdörfer and Klaus Obermayer

During slow-wave sleep, the brain produces traveling waves of slow oscillations (SOs; [MATH]), characterized by the propagation of alternating high- and low-activity states. They play a crucial role in memory consolidation and are frequently investigated, empirical…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023348] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies spike-frequency adaptation and H-current-based adaptation in a Wilson-Cowan field model of slow-wave sleep, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Understanding the mechanisms of traveling waves during slow-wave sleep, which are important for memory consolidation.
method: The authors develop a Wilson-Cowan field model incorporating spike-frequency adaptation and H-current-based adaptation, and analyze the resulting wave dynamics.
result: They show that the two adaptation mechanisms can produce equivalent wave patterns under certain conditions.
conclusion: The equivalence suggests that different biological mechanisms may underlie the same observed phenomena, aiding in model selection and interpretation.

title: Redirecting Countermoving Swarms Through Collision
authors: Jason Hindes, Chinthan B. Prasad, Loy Mcguire, And Ira B. Schwartz
abstract:
Author(s): Jason Hindes, Chinthan B. Prasad, Loy McGuire, and Ira B. Schwartz

Multiswarm systems, where two or more swarms of mobile agents occupy the same region of space with different parameters and goals, occur in a variety of biological, engineering, and defense applications. Composites of multiple swarms can produce hybrid spatiotemporal patterns, which compared to sing…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023351] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the dynamics of multiple swarms of mobile agents that collide and redirect each other, focusing on pattern formation and control.
motivation: Understanding how multiple swarms with different goals interact in the same space is important for biological, engineering, and defense applications.
method: The authors model multiswarm systems using agent-based simulations and analyze the resulting spatiotemporal patterns, particularly the effect of collisions on swarm redirection.
result: They find that collisions can lead to hybrid patterns and enable redirection of countermoving swarms, with potential for control strategies.
conclusion: Collision-mediated interactions in multiswarm systems can be harnessed for redirecting swarms, offering insights for collective behavior and robotic swarms.

title: Parametric Resonance, Chaos, And Spatial Structure In The Lotka-Volterra Model
authors: Mohamed Swailem And Alastair M. Rucklidge
abstract:
Author(s): Mohamed Swailem and Alastair M. Rucklidge

We investigate the Lotka-Volterra model for predator-prey competition with a finite carrying capacity that varies periodically in time, modeling seasonal variations in nutrients or food resources. In the absence of time variability, the ordinary differential equations have an equilibrium point that …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023352] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies parametric resonance and chaos in the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with periodic carrying capacity.
motivation: Understanding how seasonal variations affect predator-prey dynamics and spatial pattern formation.
method: Numerical simulations and bifurcation analysis of the Lotka-Volterra equations with time-periodic carrying capacity.
result: Identified parametric resonance and chaotic behavior, and characterized spatial structures in the model.
conclusion: Seasonal forcing can induce complex dynamics including chaos and spatial patterns in ecological systems.

title: Dispersed-phase Forcing Reorganizes Lagrangian Intermittency In Turbulence
authors: Zecai Zhou, Hendrik Hessenkemper, Andrew D. Bragg, And Tian Ma
abstract:
Author(s): Zecai Zhou, Hendrik Hessenkemper, Andrew D. Bragg, and Tian Ma

In single-phase turbulence, fluctuations in the Lagrangian velocity increments become more extreme as the timescale [MATH] decreases, leading to the strongest fluctuations as [MATH]. Using high-resolution three-dimensional Lagrangian particle tracking experiments, we find that for turbulent flows where …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023338] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Lagrangian intermittency in turbulent flows with dispersed particles, focusing on fluid dynamics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how dispersed-phase forcing modifies extreme fluctuations in Lagrangian velocity increments in turbulence.
method: High-resolution 3D Lagrangian particle tracking experiments in turbulent flows with dispersed particles.
result: Dispersed-phase forcing reorganizes Lagrangian intermittency, altering the statistics of extreme velocity increments.
conclusion: The presence of dispersed particles significantly changes the intermittent behavior of turbulence, with implications for multiphase flow modeling.

title: Estimating Orbital Parameters Of Direct Imaging Exoplanet Using Neural Networks
authors: Bo Liang, Chang Liu, Hanlin Song, Tianyu Zhao, Yuxiang Xu, Zihao Xiao, Manjia Liang, Minghui Du, Wei-Liang Qian, Li-E Qiang, Mingming Sun, Peng Xu, And Ziren Luo
abstract:
Author(s): Bo Liang, Chang Liu, Hanlin Song, Tianyu Zhao, Yuxiang Xu, Zihao Xiao, Manjia Liang, Minghui Du, Wei-Liang Qian, Li-e Qiang, Mingming Sun, Peng Xu, and Ziren Luo

We propose a flow-matching Markov chain Monte Carlo (FM-MCMC) algorithm for estimating the orbital parameters of exoplanetary systems, especially for those in which only one exoplanet is involved. Compared to traditional methods that rely on random sampling within the Bayesian framework, our approac…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023341] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses a flow-matching Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to estimate orbital parameters of directly imaged exoplanets.
motivation: Traditional Bayesian methods for exoplanet orbital parameter estimation rely on random sampling, which can be inefficient. The authors aim to improve efficiency and accuracy using a flow-matching approach.
method: The authors propose a flow-matching Markov chain Monte Carlo (FM-MCMC) algorithm that combines normalizing flows with MCMC to sample from the posterior distribution of orbital parameters.
result: The FM-MCMC algorithm demonstrates improved convergence and accuracy compared to standard MCMC methods on simulated and real exoplanet data.
conclusion: Flow-matching MCMC is a promising tool for exoplanet orbital parameter estimation, offering better performance than traditional sampling methods.

title: Enhanced Plasma Production By Ambipolar Electric Fields In Convergent Magnetic Fields
authors: Kazunori Takahashi, Christine Charles, Rod W. Boswell, And Antonella Caldarelli
abstract:
Author(s): Kazunori Takahashi, Christine Charles, Rod W. Boswell, and Antonella Caldarelli

Controlled unidirectional remote plasma production in a radio-frequency (rf) plasma source is demonstrated by placing magnetic nozzle throat several tens of centimeters away from the rf antenna, where a local density peak forms near the throat. The experiment indicates that the dominant electron ene…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023322] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies plasma production in a convergent magnetic field using ambipolar electric fields, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To achieve controlled unidirectional remote plasma production for applications in plasma propulsion or processing.
method: Experimental demonstration using a radio-frequency plasma source with a magnetic nozzle throat placed away from the antenna, measuring density and electron energy.
result: A local density peak forms near the throat, indicating dominant electron energization by ambipolar electric fields in the convergent magnetic field.
conclusion: Ambipolar electric fields in convergent magnetic fields can enhance plasma production, enabling remote plasma generation.

title: Proof-of-principle Experiment Of A Beam Extraction Over Millions Of Turns Using Stable Resonance Islands And Bent Crystal
authors: D. E. Veres, P. Arrutia, S. Cettour Cave, B. H. F. Lindström, M. Giovannozzi, L. E. Pauwels, F. F. van der Veken, F. M. Velotti, And G. Franchetti
abstract:
Author(s): D. E. Veres, P. Arrutia, S. Cettour Cave, B. H. F. Lindström, M. Giovannozzi, L. E. Pauwels, F. F. Van der Veken, F. M. Velotti, and G. Franchetti

A recent theoretical investigation indicated that combining particle trapping in resonance islands with planar channeling in a bent crystal may offer a promising option for a low-loss, or even septum-free, slow-extraction technique. This work reports on the successful proof-of-principle experiment conducted at the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron, in which stable islands and a bent crystal were employed to split and channel a circulating beam onto an absorber, thereby emulating slow extraction.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022055] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports a proof-of-principle experiment on beam extraction using resonance islands and a bent crystal at CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron.
motivation: To demonstrate a low-loss, septum-free slow-extraction technique for particle accelerators, combining particle trapping in resonance islands with planar channeling in a bent crystal.
method: The experiment used stable resonance islands and a bent crystal to split and channel a circulating proton beam onto an absorber, emulating slow extraction over millions of turns.
result: Successful proof-of-principle: the beam was extracted with low loss, validating the theoretical proposal.
conclusion: This technique offers a promising option for future accelerator extraction systems, potentially reducing losses and eliminating the need for a septum.

title: Super-resonance: Breaking The Bandwidth Limit Of Resonant Modes And Its Application To Flow Control
authors: Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, And Mahmoud I. Hussein
abstract:
Author(s): Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, and Mahmoud I. Hussein

Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response well beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance, enabling broadband flow stabilization among other applications.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021045] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces super-resonance, a phenomenon that breaks the bandwidth limit of resonant modes, and applies it to flow control.
motivation: Conventional resonance has a limited bandwidth, which restricts applications like flow stabilization. The authors aim to overcome this limitation.
method: The authors theoretically and experimentally demonstrate super-resonance, achieving a broadband out-of-phase response beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance.
result: Super-resonance enables broadband flow stabilization and other applications by maintaining an out-of-phase response over a wide frequency range.
conclusion: Super-resonance provides a new paradigm for resonant systems, with potential applications in flow control and beyond.

title: Erratum: Opposite Effects Of The Rotational And Translational Energy On The Rates Of Ion-Molecule Reactions Near 0 K: The ${\mathrm{D}}_{2}^{+}+{\mathrm{NH}}_{3}$ And ${\mathrm{D}}_{2}^{+}+{\mathrm{ND}}_{3}$ Reactions [Phys. Rev. X 14, 011034 (2024)]
authors: Raphaël Hahn, David Schlander, Valentina Zhelyazkova, And Frédéric Merkt
abstract:
